tests.name: Quick Check
tests.description: Timed check on Time Zones & Celestial Coordinates

questions.question: Q: How are time zones related to longitude?
questions.correctAnswer: Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours = 15° per hour. Each time zone spans roughly 15° of longitude. Moving east by 15° adds 1 hour; moving west subtracts 1 hour. The Prime Meridian at Greenwich defines the reference (GMT/UT).

questions.question: Q: What is the equatorial coordinate system?
questions.correctAnswer: A system using right ascension (RA, measured in hours east from the vernal equinox) and declination (Dec, measured in degrees from the celestial equator) to fix objects on the celestial sphere. RA is like longitude; Dec is like latitude.

questions.question: Q: What is the difference between altitude-azimuth and equatorial coordinates?
questions.correctAnswer: Alt-az coordinates (altitude above horizon, azimuth on compass) depend on the observer's location and time. Equatorial coordinates (RA, Dec) are fixed for each star and do not change with location or time (ignoring precession).

tests.name: Exam-Style Practice
tests.description: Short-answer practice on Time Zones & Celestial Coordinates

questions.question: Q: What is right ascension and how is it measured?
questions.correctAnswer: RA is the angular distance measured eastward along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox (First Point of Aries). It is expressed in hours, minutes, and seconds (0h to 24h), where 1 hour = 15°.

questions.question: Q: What is declination?
questions.correctAnswer: The angular distance of an object north (+) or south (−) of the celestial equator, measured in degrees from 0° to ±90°. Positive declination = northern celestial hemisphere; negative = southern.

questions.question: Q: When is a star at its highest point in the sky?
questions.correctAnswer: When it crosses the meridian (the great circle from north to south through the zenith). This occurs when its hour angle = 0, i.e. when local sidereal time equals the star's RA.

questions.question: Q: What happens at the International Date Line?
questions.correctAnswer: At roughly 180° longitude, the calendar date changes by one day. Crossing eastward subtracts a day; crossing westward adds a day. The line zigzags to avoid splitting countries.

questions.question: Q: What is the hour angle of a star?
questions.correctAnswer: Hour angle = local sidereal time − star's RA. It tells you how far west of the meridian the star is, measured in hours. A positive hour angle means the star has passed the meridian; negative means it is approaching it.
